# Why a scheduler exists {#sec-why-scheduler}

::: {.tldr}
Hundreds of people share the same few hundred nodes. A scheduler — **Slurm** — is the
referee: you describe a job (how many cores, how much memory, how long, which kind of node),
Slurm puts it in line, and runs it when the resources you asked for are free. You interact
with the cluster almost entirely through Slurm.
:::

## The tragedy of the commons, made concrete

Imagine 300 researchers and 300 nodes, and no referee. Everyone logs into whatever node
looks idle and starts running. Two people land on the same node and thrash its memory until
both jobs crash. Someone starts a two-week run on the node you need for a five-minute test.
Nobody can tell whether a node is free or about to be. It's chaos, and nothing finishes.

Slurm replaces "grab a node and hope" with a simple contract:

1. You **describe** the work: resources and a time limit.
2. Slurm **reserves** exactly that, on nodes that can provide it, and **accounts** for it.
3. Your job runs with those resources guaranteed and isolated from everyone else's.
4. When your time limit is up, the job ends — which is what keeps the line moving.

Everything in the rest of this book is really about writing that description well.

## The two ways to run work

**Batch jobs** (`sbatch`) are the normal mode: you write a script that says what resources
you need and what commands to run, submit it, and walk away. Slurm runs it whenever your turn
comes — maybe now, maybe in an hour — and writes the output to a file. This is how you should
run essentially all real computation. (@sec-anatomy)

**Interactive jobs** (`salloc`) give you a live shell *on a compute node* for when you need
to poke at things by hand — debugging, exploring data, developing a script. You're still
going through the scheduler and still consuming your allocation, but you get a prompt instead
of a script. (@sec-interactive)

Both run on **compute nodes**. Neither runs on the login node — that's the whole point
(@sec-cluster).

## The three questions every job answers

Whether batch or interactive, you're always telling Slurm three things:

| Question | Directive | Covered in |
|---|---|---|
| **Who pays?** (which project) | `--account` | @sec-anatomy |
| **How much, and how long?** | `--cpus-per-task`, `--mem`, `--time`, … | @sec-resources |
| **What kind of node, and how urgent?** | `--partition`, `--qos` | @sec-partitions |

Get those right and the cluster is smooth. Get them wrong and you either wait forever, get
rejected at submit time, or watch your job die halfway through. The next chapters take them
one at a time.

## A first look at the tools

You'll meet all of these properly later, but here's the vocabulary:

```bash
sbatch submit.sh        # submit a batch job
salloc ...              # get an interactive session
squeue --me             # what are my jobs doing?
scancel <jobid>         # cancel a job
sacct -j <jobid>        # after the fact: what happened, and how much did it use?
```

ARCC also ships its own friendlier wrappers — `showjobreasons` ("why isn't my job
running?"), `showuserlimits` ("what am I even allowed to ask for?"), `showpartitions`,
`sqos` — which we lean on in @sec-partitions and @sec-monitoring.

Let's write an actual job.
